d: An open protocol that standardises how AI applications connect to external tools, data and prompts.
c:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
mcp = FastMCP("tickets")
x: MCP was open-sourced by Anthropic in November 2024 and is now governed under the Linux Foundation.

d: Without a shared standard, every AI app needs a custom connector for every external system.
x: MCP reduces M × N custom integrations to M + N: each app implements a client once and each system a server once.

d: The common analogy for MCP: one standard plug shape that many tools and apps can share.
x: The USB-C analogy describes MCP as a universal connector between AI apps and capabilities.

d: A date string such as 2025-11-25 that identifies a revision of the protocol.
x: MCP spec versions are dates in YYYY-MM-DD format, changed only for backwards-incompatible changes.

d: A model feature where tool schemas are passed in an API request and the model returns a structured call for your code to execute.
x: Hosts usually convert MCP tools into function-calling tool definitions for the model they use.

d: The Linux Foundation body to which MCP was donated in December 2025 for vendor-neutral governance.
x: MCP's governance moved to a Linux Foundation foundation so no single vendor controls the standard.

d: The AI application the user interacts with; it owns the LLM, the UI and security decisions and runs one client per server.
x: The host decides what context each server receives and enforces user consent.

d: A connector inside the host that maintains a 1:1 connection with a single MCP server.
c:
async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
    await session.initialize()
x: Each MCP client talks to exactly one server.

d: A program that exposes tools, resources and prompts to MCP clients.
x: MCP servers are isolated from each other and cannot see the full conversation.

d: An MCP server launched as a subprocess on the user's machine, usually over stdio.
x: Local servers usually get credentials from environment variables rather than OAuth.

d: An MCP server running as a web service that clients reach over Streamable HTTP.
x: Remote servers typically use Streamable HTTP with OAuth-based authorization.

d: The first request a client sends, carrying its protocolVersion, capabilities and clientInfo.
x: The initialize request must not be part of a batch and comes before any other request except ping.

d: The notification the client sends after a successful initialize response to signal it is ready for normal operation.
x: The client sends notifications/initialized after receiving the server's initialize result.

d: The client proposes the latest protocol version it supports and the server replies with that version or another it supports.
x: If the client cannot support the version the server returns, it should disconnect.

d: The exchange during initialization where client and server declare which optional features they support.
x: Only features negotiated during initialization may be used in the session.

d: A capability flag meaning the sender will notify the other side when its list of tools, resources, prompts or roots changes.
x: A server declaring tools.listChanged will send notifications/tools/list_changed when its tools change.

d: The name and version of the server implementation returned in the initialize result.
x: The initialize result contains protocolVersion, capabilities, serverInfo and optional instructions.

d: Optional text in the initialize result that tells the host or model how to use the server.
x: Servers can include an instructions string in the initialize result to guide models.

d: Ending an MCP connection, done through the transport: closing stdin for stdio or closing connections and sending DELETE for HTTP.
x: MCP defines no special shutdown message; the transport is used to end the connection.

d: The lightweight remote-procedure-call message format that all MCP messages use.
x: Every MCP message includes "jsonrpc": "2.0".

d: A JSON-RPC message with an id and a method that expects a response.
x: MCP request ids must be strings or integers and never null.

d: A JSON-RPC message that carries the same id as a request and either a result or an error.
x: A response contains either result or error, never both.

d: A one-way JSON-RPC message with a method but no id, which gets no reply.
x: Notifications have no id field and must not be answered.

d: Sending several JSON-RPC messages as one array, which MCP removed in the 2025-06-18 revision.
x: Since 2025-06-18, MCP does not support JSON-RPC batch arrays.

d: The JSON-RPC error returned when the method does not exist or its capability was not negotiated.
x: Calling an unsupported method returns error code -32601.

d: The JSON-RPC error for bad arguments, such as an unknown tool name or missing required parameter.
x: An unknown tool name in tools/call is reported as a protocol error with code -32602.

d: The JSON-RPC error returned when the received text is not valid JSON.
x: Invalid JSON produces error code -32700.

d: The MCP-specific error code returned when resources/read is asked for a URI that does not exist.
x: MCP uses error code -32002 for a missing resource.

d: A request either side can send to check that the connection is alive; the receiver replies with an empty result.
x: Either the client or the server may send ping.

d: notifications/progress messages sent for a long request, identified by the progressToken the requester placed in params._meta.
x: Progress is only sent if the requester included a progressToken in the request's _meta.

d: notifications/cancelled, sent with the requestId of an in-flight request the sender no longer needs.
x: A cancelled request is identified by its requestId in notifications/cancelled.

d: Splitting list results into pages: the result includes nextCursor, which the client sends back as cursor.
x: A missing nextCursor in a list result means there are no more pages.

d: The utility where servers send notifications/message log entries and clients set the minimum level with logging/setLevel.
x: MCP log levels follow syslog severities such as debug, info, warning and error.

d: The request that asks a server to suggest values for a prompt argument or resource-template variable.
x: Servers declare the completions capability to support argument autocompletion.

d: A reserved field on many MCP objects for extra metadata such as progress tokens.
x: The progressToken is placed in the params._meta object of a request.

d: A function a server exposes for the model to call, described by a name, description and JSON Schema for its input.
x: Tools are model-controlled: the LLM decides when to call them, with the user able to approve.

d: The request a client sends to discover the tools a server offers.
x: tools/list results can be paginated with nextCursor.

d: The request a client sends to invoke a tool with a name and arguments.
x: tools/call params contain the tool name and an arguments object.

d: The JSON Schema object that describes a tool's arguments.
x: A tool's inputSchema must be a JSON Schema whose type is object.

d: An optional JSON Schema describing the structuredContent a tool returns.
x: If a tool declares an outputSchema, its results must include structuredContent that conforms to it.

d: A JSON object in a tool result holding machine-readable output, alongside the content array.
x: For backwards compatibility, tools returning structuredContent should also include the serialized JSON in a text content block.

d: A flag in a tool result marking a tool execution failure, so the model can see the error and retry.
c: {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Date must be in the future"}], "isError": true}
x: Tool execution errors are returned as results with isError true rather than as JSON-RPC errors.

d: An item in a tool result's content array, such as text, image, audio, resource_link or an embedded resource.
x: Image and audio content blocks carry base64 data plus a mimeType.

d: A content block in a tool result that points to a resource by URI instead of embedding its contents.
x: A resource_link lets the client read the resource later with resources/read.

d: Optional hints such as readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint describing a tool's behaviour.
x: Clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.

d: A tool annotation meaning the tool does not modify its environment; it defaults to false.
x: readOnlyHint defaults to false when it is not specified.

d: A tool annotation meaning the tool may perform destructive updates; it defaults to true and only matters when the tool is not read-only.
x: destructiveHint defaults to true for tools that are not read-only.

d: A tool annotation meaning repeated calls with the same arguments have no additional effect; it defaults to false.
x: idempotentHint defaults to false.

d: A tool annotation meaning the tool interacts with an open world of external entities such as the web; it defaults to true.
x: openWorldHint defaults to true.

d: The notification a server sends when its set of available tools changes.
x: After notifications/tools/list_changed, the client should call tools/list again.

d: Natural-language text explaining what a tool does and when to use it, which the model reads to choose tools.
x: Clear, distinct tool descriptions improve the model's tool selection.

d: A piece of data identified by a URI, such as a file, schema or record, that a server exposes for reading as context.
x: Resources are application-controlled: the host decides what to read and attach as context.

d: The request a client sends to fetch the contents of a resource by URI.
x: resources/read returns a contents array whose items have either text or a base64 blob.

d: The request a client sends to list a server's concrete resources, with pagination.
x: resources/list returns resources with fields such as uri, name, mimeType and description.

d: A parameterised resource definition using an RFC 6570 URI template such as weather://forecast/{city}.
x: Resource templates are discovered with resources/templates/list.

d: The base64-encoded field used for binary resource contents such as images or PDFs.
x: Binary resource contents are returned as base64 in a blob field.

d: A client asking with resources/subscribe to be told via notifications/resources/updated when a resource changes.
x: Servers declare resources.subscribe to support subscriptions.

d: Optional hints on resources: audience (user or assistant), priority from 0 to 1, and lastModified.
x: A resource priority of 1.0 means the resource is effectively required.

d: A reusable, parameterised message template a server exposes for the user to choose, often shown as a slash command.
x: Prompts are user-controlled: the user explicitly selects them.

d: The request that fetches a prompt by name with arguments and returns a list of role-tagged messages.
x: prompts/get returns messages whose role is user or assistant.

d: A client feature where a server asks the host's LLM to generate a completion via sampling/createMessage.
x: With sampling, the host keeps control over which model runs and can let the user review the request.

d: Advisory sampling hints: model-name hints plus costPriority, speedPriority and intelligencePriority values from 0 to 1.
x: The client makes the final model choice; model preferences are only advisory.

d: URIs, usually file:// folders, that a client exposes to tell a server which parts of the filesystem are in scope.
x: Clients send notifications/roots/list_changed when the set of roots changes.

d: A client feature where a server asks the user for extra structured input through the host via elicitation/create.
x: Elicitation was added to MCP in the 2025-06-18 revision.

d: The restricted JSON Schema in a form-mode elicitation: a flat object whose properties are primitive types.
x: Elicitation schemas only allow flat objects with string, number, integer, boolean or enum properties.

d: The three outcomes of an elicitation request: accept with data, decline, or cancel.
x: decline means the user explicitly refused, while cancel means they dismissed without choosing.

d: Elicitation that sends the user to an external URL, so sensitive data such as credentials or payments never passes through the client.
x: URL-mode elicitation was added in the 2025-11-25 revision for sensitive interactions.

d: An experimental 2025-11-25 feature that turns a long-running request into a task with an id that can be polled for status and results later.
x: Tasks follow a "call now, fetch later" pattern.

d: The transport where the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over stdin and stdout.
x: On stdio, the server must not write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message.

d: Writing diagnostic logs to standard error so stdout stays reserved for protocol messages.
x: stdio servers may write UTF-8 logs to stderr.

d: The remote transport introduced in 2025-03-26: one endpoint where clients POST messages and servers reply with JSON or an SSE stream.
x: Streamable HTTP replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport that used two endpoints.

d: The deprecated 2024-11-05 remote transport that used a separate SSE endpoint and a POST endpoint.
x: Servers can serve the legacy HTTP+SSE endpoints alongside Streamable HTTP for older clients.

d: A one-way HTTP streaming format (text/event-stream) a Streamable HTTP server can use to send several messages back.
x: A server may answer a POST with an SSE stream that ends after the final response.

d: An HTTP header a Streamable HTTP server may assign in the initialize response, which the client then sends on every request.
x: When a server returns 404 for a session ID, the client must start a new session with initialize.

d: The HTTP header the client sends on every request after initialization to state the negotiated protocol version.
x: Over Streamable HTTP, clients send the MCP-Protocol-Version header on later requests.

d: The HTTP status a Streamable HTTP server returns, with no body, when the POST contained only a notification or response.
x: If a POST carries a notification, the server replies 202 Accepted with no body.

d: Recovering a dropped SSE stream: the client reconnects with Last-Event-ID so the server can replay missed events.
x: Servers attach event ids to SSE events so streams can be resumed.

d: Checking the HTTP Origin header on every request, which Streamable HTTP servers must do to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.
x: Local HTTP MCP servers should bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0.

d: The high-level Python API (in the official SDK as mcp.server.fastmcp) that turns decorated functions into tools, resources and prompts.
x: FastMCP builds a tool's inputSchema from type hints and its description from the docstring.

d: The FastMCP decorator that registers a function as a resource or resource template for a URI pattern.
x: A placeholder in the URI pattern, such as {name}, becomes a function parameter.

d: The FastMCP decorator that registers a function returning a prompt template.
x: Functions decorated with @mcp.prompt become prompts users can choose in the host.

d: The FastMCP Context parameter that gives a tool logging, progress reporting, resource reads, elicitation and sampling.
c:
async def process(files: list[str], ctx: Context) -> str:
    await ctx.report_progress(progress=1, total=len(files))
x: Adding a parameter typed Context gives a tool access to ctx.info and ctx.report_progress.

d: The Python SDK class that runs the client side of an MCP connection: initialize, list_tools, call_tool, read_resource and more.
c:
async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
    await session.initialize()
    result = await session.call_tool("add", {"a": 2, "b": 3})
x: A client must await session.initialize() before listing or calling tools.

d: The Python SDK context manager that launches a server subprocess and yields read and write streams.
x: stdio_client takes StdioServerParameters with the command and args used to start the server.

d: The Python SDK context manager for connecting to a remote server over Streamable HTTP.
x: streamablehttp_client is imported from mcp.client.streamable_http.

d: The official developer tool with a web UI for connecting to a server, listing and calling tools, reading resources and watching messages.
x: The Inspector can be started with npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector or with mcp dev server.py.

d: The Claude Desktop configuration file where local MCP servers are registered under the mcpServers key.
x: Each mcpServers entry gives a command, args and optional env for launching the server.

d: The official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk package with McpServer, registerTool and transports such as StdioServerTransport.
c:
const server = new McpServer({ name: "demo", version: "1.0.0" });
await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
x: The TypeScript SDK commonly uses zod schemas to define tool inputs.

d: The package that loads tools from MCP servers as LangChain and LangGraph tools.
x: MultiServerMCPClient can connect to several MCP servers and return their tools for an agent.

d: The optional OAuth 2.1-based framework for HTTP transports, in which the MCP server acts as a resource server that validates access tokens.
x: stdio servers should take credentials from the environment instead of following the HTTP authorization spec.

d: A document (RFC 9728) at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource that tells clients which authorization server protects an MCP server.
x: MCP servers must implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata for authorization discovery.

d: The header in a 401 response that points the client at the server's protected resource metadata.
x: An unauthenticated request to a protected MCP server receives 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header.

d: Proof Key for Code Exchange, which MCP clients must use in the OAuth authorization-code flow, with the S256 method.
x: MCP requires PKCE for all clients, including confidential ones.

d: The OAuth resource parameter clients send so access tokens are bound to the specific MCP server they are meant for.
x: Clients include the resource parameter in authorization and token requests.

d: The forbidden anti-pattern where an MCP server accepts tokens not issued for it or forwards the client's token to upstream APIs.
x: MCP servers must only accept tokens issued specifically for them.

d: A client-registration approach (preferred since 2025-11-25) where the client_id is an HTTPS URL that points to a JSON document describing the client.
x: Client ID Metadata Documents let clients register without a prior manual step with every authorization server.

d: OAuth RFC 7591, which lets a client register itself with an authorization server automatically.
x: Dynamic Client Registration is an optional fallback registration method in MCP.

d: An attack where malicious instructions are hidden in a tool's description or metadata to manipulate the model.
x: Hosts should show users full tool descriptions and only install servers from trusted sources.

d: An attack where content returned by a tool, such as a web page or email, contains instructions the model then follows.
x: Tool outputs should be treated as untrusted data, not instructions.

d: An attack where a server changes its tool definitions after the user approved them.
x: Detecting changed tool definitions and re-approving them mitigates rug pulls.

d: A problem where a privileged proxy server acts on behalf of a client that should not have that access.
x: Per-client consent and proper token audience checks defend against confused deputy attacks.

d: Two servers exposing tools with the same name, which can confuse the model or let one server shadow another.
x: Prefixing tools with the server name, such as github__create_issue, avoids collisions.

d: The dangerous combination of access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to send data out.
x: Limiting combinations of tools reduces data-exfiltration risk.

d: The official open catalogue of public MCP servers at registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, where each server is described by a server.json.
x: The MCP Registry launched in preview in September 2025.

d: A proxy between hosts and many MCP servers that centralises auth, policy, audit logging, rate limits and tool filtering.
x: Gateways give enterprises central audit logs and access control over many servers.

d: A protocol for agents to communicate with other agents across vendors using Agent Cards and tasks.
x: MCP connects agents to tools and data, while A2A connects agents to agents.

d: Granting servers and tokens only the minimum scopes, tools and roots needed for the task.
x: Read-only tools and narrowly scoped tokens reduce the damage from a compromised agent.
